entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Benedict V, elected Pope in 964, represented a fleeting but defiant assertion of Roman autonomy against the burgeoning Ottonian Holy Roman Empire during the turbulent Saeculum obscurum. His short reign, lasting just over a month from May 22 to June 23, 964, pitted the will of the Roman clergy and people against the formidable power of Emperor Otto I, who had previously deposed John XII and installed Leo VIII. This struggle for papal legitimacy highlighted the deep-seated tensions between imperial authority and the aspirations for ecclesiastical independence in 10th-century Italy, making Benedict V a symbol of a brief resistance against imperial domination of the papacy.

Following the death of Pope John XII, who had been restored after Otto I's departure from Rome, the Roman populace, rejecting the imperial-appointed Leo VIII, elected Benedict, then a cardinal-deacon, on May 22, 964. This act directly defied Otto I's decree that no pope could be elected without imperial consent. Upon hearing of this, Emperor Otto I swiftly marched on Rome, besieging the city. After a month of resistance, the Romans, facing starvation, surrendered Benedict V to the Emperor. On June 23, 964, in a synod held at the Lateran, Benedict was formally stripped of his pontifical vestments, his pallium ripped from him by Leo VIII, and he was degraded from the priesthood to the rank of deacon.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Benedict V's election and swift deposition underscored the profound struggle for power between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire, marking a critical moment in the definition of papal sovereignty. His fate exemplified the challenges to ecclesiastical independence during the Ottonian period, influencing later reforms aimed at freeing the church from secular control.
